2 Peter 1.summary: Second Peter opens with a greeting from ‘Simeon Peter, a servant and apostle of Jesus Christ’ to people who have received ‘a faith of equal standing’ with the apostles’ own, through the righteousness of ‘our God and Savior Jesus Christ.’ He prays that grace and peace will be multiplied to them in the knowledge of God and of Jesus. Peter explains that God’s divine power has given believers everything needed for life and godliness through the knowledge of the one who called them, and has given ‘precious and very great promises’ so that they may ‘become partakers of the divine nature, having escaped from the corruption that is in the world because of sinful desire.’ In response he urges them to make every effort to add to their faith a series of qualities: virtue, knowledge, self-control, steadfastness, godliness, brotherly affection, and love. If these qualities are increasing, they will keep believers from being ineffective or unfruitful in the knowledge of Christ, while someone who lacks them is nearsighted and has forgotten that he was cleansed from his former sins. Peter urges them to be diligent to make their ‘calling and election’ sure, promising that if they practice these things they will never fall and will be richly welcomed into the eternal kingdom of the Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. Peter says he will keep reminding them of these things, even though they know them, as long as he is in ‘this body,’ since he knows his departure is coming soon, as the Lord Jesus made clear to him, and he will make every effort so they can recall these things after his death. He then insists that he and the other apostles did not follow ‘cleverly devised myths’ when they made known the power and coming of the Lord Jesus Christ, but were eyewitnesses of his majesty. He describes hearing the voice from ‘the Majestic Glory’ say ‘This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased,’ when he was with Jesus ‘on the holy mountain.’ This, he says, makes the prophetic word more fully confirmed, and readers do well to pay attention to it ‘as to a lamp shining in a dark place’ until the day dawns and the morning star rises in their hearts. He closes the chapter by stating that no prophecy of Scripture comes from someone’s ‘own interpretation,’ for no prophecy was ever produced by the will of man, but men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit.
2 Peter 1.whereWeAre:
Peter says he expects to die soon, ‘as our Lord Jesus Christ made clear to me’ (1:14). Many interpreters connect this with Jesus’s words to Peter about how he would die in John 21:18-19. The letter does not say.

Early Christian tradition says Peter was killed in Rome, probably under Nero. This is reported by Clement of Rome (1 Clement 5), by Dionysius of Corinth and Tertullian as reported by Eusebius (Church History 2.25), and in later writings. The details of his death are traditional and cannot be independently verified. Tacitus (Annals 15.44) records that Nero executed Christians in Rome after the fire of AD 64 but does not mention Peter.

The Transfiguration is described in Matthew 17:1-8, Mark 9:2-8, and Luke 9:28-36. Matthew and Mark place it ‘on a high mountain’ (Luke: ‘the mountain’) with Peter, James, and John present and a voice saying, ‘This is my beloved Son.’ Peter’s wording in 1:17 resembles (Matthew 17:5). The Gospels do not name the mountain.

The early church was slow to accept 2 Peter universally; the first clear mention comes from Origen (3rd century). Origen, as reported by Eusebius (Church History 6.25), said Peter left one acknowledged letter and possibly a second, since it was doubted, and Eusebius (3.3) says it was not generally accepted as part of the canon but many found it useful. Jerome (On Illustrious Men 1) notes that many doubted its authenticity because of differences in style from 1 Peter. It appears in the canon list of Athanasius (AD 367) and was affirmed by later councils.

The letter reflects a world in which Christians faced teachers who denied or mocked Christian teaching (see chapters 2–3). Chapter 1 prepares for this by affirming the reliability of the apostolic message. Peter’s emphasis on remembering, eyewitness testimony, and the source of prophecy makes sense in a setting where false teachers were challenging the apostolic message, as the next two chapters show. The note of urgency in 1:12-15 fits the letter’s form as a kind of farewell or testament, a form familiar from Jewish and early Christian writings.

keyFigures.name: Simeon Peter (the author)
keyFigures.role: He greets the readers, urges godly growth, gives an apostolic reminder, and appeals to his eyewitness experience. The letter’s authority rests on his apostolic standing and eyewitness testimony.

keyFigures.name: The readers (‘those who have obtained a faith of equal standing’)
keyFigures.role: They are urged to grow in character and remember the apostolic message. They have received the same kind of faith as the apostles, by the gift of God.

keyFigures.name: Jesus Christ (‘our God and Savior,’ ‘our Lord’)
keyFigures.role: He is the center of the faith and hope described, and the one whose majesty Peter witnessed. Everything in the chapter flows from knowing and following him.

keyFigures.name: God the Father (‘the Majestic Glory’)
keyFigures.role: He confirms Jesus as his beloved Son. His testimony supports the apostolic message.

keyFigures.name: The other apostles (‘we’)
keyFigures.role: They share Peter’s eyewitness testimony. It shows that the apostolic message rests on shared testimony.

keyFigures.name: The prophets (‘men who spoke from God’)
keyFigures.role: They are described as carried along by the Holy Spirit. They establish the reliability of Scripture’s prophetic message.

keyFigures.name: The Holy Spirit
keyFigures.role: He is the divine source of prophecy. He grounds Scripture’s authority.

keyFigures.name: James and John
keyFigures.role: They are not mentioned in 2 Peter 1. Their presence helps identify who ‘we’ refers to in 1:16-18.

keyFigures.name: Moses and Elijah
keyFigures.role: They are not mentioned in 2 Peter 1. They provide the Gospel context of the event Peter recalls.

keyThemes.explanation:
God’s divine power has granted everything needed for life and godliness, and given precious and very great promises.

The text presents effort and obedience as responses to God’s gifts and not as ways to earn them.

Believers are told to add virtue, knowledge, self-control, steadfastness, godliness, brotherly affection, and love to their faith.

The passage encourages ongoing growth, with love as the culmination.

keyThemes.theme: Perseverance and the hope of Christ’s kingdom
keyThemes.explanation:
Diligence in these things keeps believers from stumbling and leads to rich entry into the eternal kingdom.

The text presents steadfastness as part of the Christian life.

keyThemes.theme: The reliability of the apostolic testimony
keyThemes.explanation:
Peter says the apostles did not follow cleverly devised myths but were eyewitnesses of Christ’s majesty, hearing the voice from heaven.

The text invites readers to trust the apostolic testimony as grounded in actual experience.

The prophetic word is a lamp in a dark place, and no prophecy was produced by human will but by people carried along by the Holy Spirit.

The text grounds the reliability of Scripture in the Spirit’s work.

2 Peter 2.summary: Peter reminds his readers that just as there were false prophets among the people of Israel, there will be false teachers among them. These teachers will secretly introduce destructive heresies, even denying ‘the Master who bought them,’ and bring swift destruction on themselves. Many will follow their sensuality, and because of them the way of truth will be spoken of with contempt. Out of greed they will exploit the readers with false words. But their condemnation, Peter says, has long been in place and is not asleep. To show that judgment is certain and that God also rescues the godly, Peter gives three examples. God did not spare angels who sinned but put them in chains of darkness until judgment. He did not spare the ancient world but brought a flood on the ungodly while preserving Noah, ‘a herald of righteousness,’ and seven others. And he condemned Sodom and Gomorrah to ashes as an example for the ungodly, while rescuing righteous Lot, who was distressed by the lawless conduct around him. From these Peter concludes that the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trials and to keep the unrighteous under punishment until the day of judgment, especially those who follow defiling desires and despise authority. He then describes the false teachers in strong terms: bold and willful, they slander glorious beings, though even angels do not do this; they are like unreasoning animals, they revel in the daytime, they have eyes full of adultery, they entice unstable people, and their hearts are trained in greed. They have followed the way of Balaam, son of Beor (or Bosor), who loved gain from wrongdoing and was rebuked by a speaking donkey. They are waterless springs and mists driven by a storm, for whom the gloom of utter darkness is reserved. They speak loud, empty boasts, entice people who are barely escaping error with sensual desires, and promise freedom while being slaves of corruption themselves. Peter says that if people escape the world’s defilements through knowing Christ and are then entangled again, their last state is worse than the first. It would have been better never to have known the way of righteousness than to turn back from the holy commandment. He ends with two proverbs: ‘The dog returns to its own vomit,’ and ‘the sow, after washing, returns to wallow in the mire.’
2 Peter 2.whereWeAre:
Itinerant teachers and philosophers were common in the Greco-Roman world. Some were criticized by ancient writers for seeking money. Christians also had traveling teachers and prophets, and early guidance, such as the Didache (chapters 11–12), told churches to test them and watch for those who sought gain.

Churches often met in homes and shared meals together (compare 1 Corinthians 11:17-34). In 2:13, the teachers ‘feast with you,’ which indicates they were present in the community’s gatherings. Jude 1:12 has a parallel about ‘love feasts.’ Note that 2:13 has a textual variant (‘deceptions’ or ‘love feasts’), and the ESV follows ‘deceits’; Jude 1:12 itself is not in doubt.

Jewish traditions outside the Old Testament expanded the stories of the fallen angels (1 Enoch 6–16), of Noah as a preacher (for example Josephus, Antiquities 1.74), and of Balaam. The letter’s examples would have been familiar to readers who knew such traditions, though the letter relies on the Old Testament accounts.

The destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah is described in Genesis 19:24-28. Ancient writers, including Strabo (Geography 16.2.44) and Tacitus (Histories 5.7), describe burned land near the Dead Sea: Strabo reports a local tradition of Sodom and other burned cities there, while Tacitus describes a scorched plain once holding great cities, which he says lightning burned, without naming Sodom.

Some scholars compare the false teachers’ teaching about ‘freedom’ (2:19) with later libertine groups, but the letter itself does not identify the movement. The letter’s examples of flood, angels, and Sodom all concern people who ignored warnings, which responds to the mockery of judgment that the author expects from the false teachers (3:3-4). The emphasis on greed fits a world where traveling teachers were often paid, and the warning about feasts fits churches that met around shared meals.

keyFigures.name: The false teachers
keyFigures.role: They are the subject of the warning and judgment. The letter’s readers are warned about their danger and their certain judgment.

keyFigures.name: The false prophets of Israel's past
keyFigures.role: They provide a parallel to the coming false teachers. False teaching is not a new problem.

keyFigures.name: The Master (Jesus Christ)
keyFigures.role: He is the one the false teachers deny. Denying him is the central charge.

keyFigures.name: The readers
keyFigures.role: They are warned and assured. They are the ones the false teachers will exploit.

keyFigures.name: The angels who sinned
keyFigures.role: They are the first example of judgment. Even exalted beings are judged.

keyFigures.name: Noah and ‘seven others’
keyFigures.role: They are the example of God preserving the righteous in judgment. God rescues his own even as he judges the ungodly.

keyFigures.name: The ancient world (the ungodly)
keyFigures.role: They are the second example of judgment. Judgment came on a world that seemed secure.

keyFigures.name: Sodom and Gomorrah
keyFigures.role: They are the third example, ‘an example of what is going to happen to the ungodly.’. They show the end of lawless living.

keyFigures.name: Lot
keyFigures.role: He is rescued from Sodom's destruction. He illustrates that the Lord rescues the godly from trials.

keyFigures.name: ‘The glorious ones’
keyFigures.role: They are the object of the teachers’ slander, in contrast to angels who do not slander them. It shows the arrogance of the teachers.

keyFigures.name: Balaam, son of Beor (Bosor)
keyFigures.role: His ‘way’ is the model for the teachers’ greed. He shows how profit can corrupt a prophet.

keyFigures.name: The speaking donkey
keyFigures.role: It rebuked the prophet’s madness. Even a donkey restrained Balaam’s folly.

keyFigures.name: Those who are barely escaping from those who live in error
keyFigures.role: They are the targets of the teachers’ promises. They show who is at risk.

keyThemes.explanation:
False teachers secretly introduce destructive heresies, deny the Master, and lead many astray.

The text calls readers to be alert to teaching that undermines Christ and promotes immorality.

God did not spare sinning angels, the ancient world, or Sodom and Gomorrah.

The text treats God’s judgment as sure.

Noah and Lot were preserved, and ‘the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trials.’

The text offers assurance to believers under pressure.

The false teachers are greedy, sensual, and arrogant, following the way of Balaam.

The text suggests that character is part of how to evaluate teachers.

The teachers promise freedom while being slaves of corruption; ‘whatever overcomes a person, to that he is enslaved.’

The text warns that going back to former ways leads to worse bondage.

explainedReferences.explanation: Peter quotes the proverb about a dog returning to its vomit.

2 Peter 3.summary: The author says this is his second letter to the same readers and that both letters aim to stir them up to remember what the holy prophets and the apostles taught (2 Peter 3:1-2). He then warns that in the last days scoffers will come, living by their own desires and mocking the promise of Christ's coming by saying that nothing has changed since the ancestors died (2 Peter 3:3-4). He answers that they willfully ignore that God's word created the heavens and earth and that the world that then existed was destroyed by water; by the same word the present heavens and earth are being kept for fire and for the day of judgment of the ungodly (2 Peter 3:5-7). Addressing his readers as 'beloved,' he adds that the Lord's timescale is not ours ('one day is as a thousand years'), that the delay is patience rather than slowness, and that God does not wish any to perish but all to reach repentance (2 Peter 3:8-9). The day of the Lord will come like a thief, with the heavens passing away and the heavenly bodies (or ‘elements’) dissolving, and he urges holy and godly living while awaiting new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells (2 Peter 3:10-13). He closes by urging peace, diligence and being found without spot, counting the Lord's patience as salvation, noting that Paul's letters contain things hard to understand that the ignorant and unstable twist, and ending with a final charge to be on guard and to grow in the grace and knowledge of the Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, to whom be glory now and to the day of eternity (2 Peter 3:14-18).
2 Peter 3.whereWeAre:
Some people were mocking the promise of Christ's return and appealing to the death of 'the fathers' and the continuity of the world as evidence.

The author answers by pointing to creation, the flood, God's patience and the coming day of the Lord, and by urging holy living.

Paul's letters were already circulating among the readers and were being compared with 'the other Scriptures.' The text does not say which letters or how widely they were collected.

Some early Christians seem to have felt anxious about the delay of Christ's return as the first generation passed away (if that is what 'the fathers' of 3:4 means). Other New Testament writings also address this concern, for example 1 Thessalonians 4:13-18 and John 21:22-23.

Scoffers' arguments resemble general ancient ideas of a stable, unchanging cosmos. Some philosophical schools, such as Epicureans, denied divine intervention in the world, and Stoics expected the cosmos to be periodically consumed by fire (ekpyrosis). Whether the scoffers were influenced by any particular school is not known, and the author's picture of judgment by fire is grounded in Scripture and Jewish tradition rather than in Stoicism. The chapter responds to a specific historical challenge: on one reading of 'the fathers' (3:4), the first generation had died and Christ had not yet returned. The author draws on Old Testament history (creation, the flood) and on the Psalms (Psalm 90:4), the prophets (new heavens and earth, compare Isaiah 65:17 and 66:22) and the apostles, including Paul, to answer it.

keyFigures.name: The author ('Peter' in 1:1)
keyFigures.role: Reminds his readers, warns them about scoffers, answers the doubt about Christ's return, and exhorts them to holy living and growth. Speaks with pastoral concern ('beloved,' used four times in the chapter) and with authority; his purpose is stated as stirring up sincere minds by way of reminder.

keyFigures.name: The readers ('beloved')
keyFigures.role: They are urged to remember, not to be misled, to live holy lives, and to grow in grace and knowledge. The chapter's application is mainly addressed to them as people waiting for Christ's return.

keyFigures.name: The scoffers
keyFigures.role: Mock the promise of Christ's coming by claiming nothing has changed since creation. Their challenge prompts the author's teaching about God's word, the flood, divine patience, and the coming day.

keyFigures.name: The Lord and Savior (Jesus Christ)
keyFigures.role: His promised coming is what the scoffers mock, and the day of the Lord is what believers await. Readers are told to grow in knowledge of him, and the doxology is given to him. The chapter is framed around the promise of his coming and ends with glory ascribed to him.

keyFigures.name: God
keyFigures.role: Acts as creator, judge, and patient saviour; his promise of new heavens and a new earth is what believers wait for. The argument rests on God's word as reliable both in creation and judgment and on his patient character.

keyFigures.name: The holy prophets
keyFigures.role: Their words are the first of two authorities the author cites. Links the hope of the Lord's coming to the older Scriptures; see also 1:19-21.

keyFigures.name: The apostles
keyFigures.role: Their teaching is the second authority the author cites. Shows the author placing apostolic teaching beside the prophets.

keyFigures.name: The fathers
keyFigures.role: Cited by the scoffers as evidence that nothing has changed. Their deaths are the basis of the scoffers' argument that the promise has failed.

keyFigures.name: Paul
keyFigures.role: The author says Paul wrote to the readers with the wisdom given him, that his letters contain things hard to understand, and that some twist them. Shows that the author knew several of Paul's letters ('all his letters') and ranked them with 'the other Scriptures'; the extent of their circulation is not stated, nor is how much of Paul's output the author knew.

keyFigures.name: The ignorant and unstable
keyFigures.role: Serve as a warning of what can happen when Scripture is misread. Underlines the need for stability and sound understanding.

keyFigures.name: The lawless
keyFigures.role: Represent the danger the readers are told to guard against. The warning leads into the closing call to grow in grace and knowledge.

keyFigures.name: Noah and the flood generation
keyFigures.role: The flood is used as proof that God's word has acted in judgment and that things have not always continued unchanged. Provides the precedent for the coming judgment by fire.

keyThemes.theme: The reliability of God's word and promise
keyThemes.explanation:
The author reminds the readers of the prophets and apostles (3:2) and argues that God's word created the heavens and earth, brought judgment by water, and now holds the present heavens and earth for fire (3:5-7). The promise of Christ's coming rests on the same word.

Doubts about God's promises can be met by remembering what God has already said and done.

keyThemes.theme: Divine patience and the call to repentance
keyThemes.explanation:
The apparent delay is explained as patience: the Lord is 'not slow' but 'patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance.' The readers are told to count that patience as salvation.

God's timing is purposeful and merciful, and time should be used for repentance and faithful living.

keyThemes.theme: The certainty of judgment and the coming day of the Lord
keyThemes.explanation:
The present heavens and earth are being kept for fire until the day of judgment and destruction of the ungodly (3:7). The day of the Lord will come like a thief, and everything will be dissolved or exposed (3:10-12).

The coming day should shape how people live now.

keyThemes.theme: Holy living and hope in the new creation
keyThemes.explanation:
Because everything will be dissolved, the readers should live 'lives of holiness and godliness,' wait for the day of God, and look for 'new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells.' They are to be diligent to be found 'without spot or blemish, and at peace.'

Hope for God's coming kingdom is meant to shape character and conduct in the present.

keyThemes.theme: Stability, sound understanding of Scripture, and growth in grace
keyThemes.explanation:
The author notes that Paul's letters contain things 'hard to understand' that the ignorant and unstable twist, as they do the other Scriptures, and warns the readers not to be carried away by the error of the lawless. The closing charge is to 'grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.'

Careful, humble reading of Scripture and continual growth in Christ guard against error.
